Neonatal Undulate rays emerge from their egg cases after an incubation period that is strongly temperature-dependent. At a consistent water temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C], the embryonic development period extends to approximately 9 months [ab = approximately 9 months], reflecting the relatively slow metabolic rates characteristic of many batoid elasmobranchs. Upon hatching, neonates measure about 13 cm [Lb = about 13 cm] in total length, a size that allows them to immediately commence benthic foraging on small crustaceans. This length at birth is modest compared to the maximum asymptotic size the species can attain, but it represents a well-provisioned developmental stage. The relatively long gestation and the investment in a single, well-developed offspring are typical of the life-history strategy seen in many rajiform skates, where low fecundity is balanced by higher juvenile survivorship. Observations from captive breeding programmes indicate that these early life stages are particularly sensitive to thermal fluctuations, and maintaining stable temperatures around 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C] is crucial for successful yolk-sac resorption and the onset of independent foraging. The age at birth thus constitutes a critical life-history bottleneck.

As Undulate rays progress through the juvenile and sub-adult phases, somatic growth proceeds steadily until individuals approach the size thresholds associated with sexual maturation. Field surveys and captive growth studies have shown that puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, is attained at a total length of 86.2 cm [Lp = 86.2 cm]. This length at puberty represents a substantial proportion of the species' theoretical ultimate total length, which has been estimated at 100 cm [Li = 100 cm], indicating that reproductive activation occurs relatively late in the growth trajectory. Males and females appear to mature at similar sizes, though detailed histological analyses of testicular and ovarian development are still limited for wild populations. The length at sexual maturity is an important parameter for stock assessment models, as it directly influences the reproductive potential of the population. Reaching 86.2 cm [Lp = 86.2 cm] in total length typically requires several years of sustained growth. Compared to other sympatric skate species within the Rajidae family, the length at puberty for Raja undulata is intermediate, reflecting a moderate pace of life-history development that is well-suited to the continental shelf environments it inhabits.

The reproductive output of mature female Undulate rays has been characterised through both captive observations and analyses of oviducal gland and ovarian activity in landed specimens. When maintained at a stable thermal regime of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C], females deposit egg cases throughout the year, producing between 62 and 124 eggs annually [Ri = between 62 and 124 eggs annually]. This annual fecundity is moderate for a skate of this body size, constrained by the large, well-yolked eggs that are deposited in protective egg cases. The maximum reproductive rate recorded under these captive conditions, which serve as a proxy for the species' potential in a favourable environment, is 124 eggs per year [Ri = 124 eggs per year]. The characteristic of depositing eggs continuously over many months rather than in a single, pulsed event is a reproductive strategy that may buffer against annual variability in prey availability for the emerging neonates. The egg cases themselves are large and leathery, providing mechanical protection and a sustained yolk supply for the developing embryo during the lengthy incubation. These life-history traits contribute to the species' resilience under moderate fishing pressure.

The ultimate body size achieved by the Undulate ray has been a subject of interest for fisheries biologists, given its implications for biomass and fecundity. The maximum recorded wet weight for a large adult individual is approximately 7,590 grams [Wwi = approximately 7,590 grams], though this value is derived from the relationship between length and mass rather than from a single exceptionally large specimen. This asymptotic body mass corresponds to the ultimate total length of 100 cm [Li = 100 cm], beyond which further somatic growth is negligible. The relationship between length and mass is typical for rajiform skates. A female of this size would be expected to have the highest fecundity, contributing the maximum number of eggs annually. The largest individuals are presumably the oldest and most experienced breeders within the population, having survived the various sources of natural and fishing mortality that structure the age distribution. Protecting these large, highly fecund individuals is often a management priority for elasmobranch conservation.

Longevity estimates for the Undulate ray have been derived from tagging studies and from quantitative analyses of growth bands in vertebral centra. Under natural thermal conditions averaging 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C], the maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years], a duration that is typical for a skate of this body size and maturation schedule. This relatively extended lifespan, combined with a late age at puberty and low fecundity, renders the species vulnerable to overexploitation, as population recovery from depletion can be slow. The maximum lifespan of 13 years [am = 13 years] places Raja undulata in a moderate position among its congeners; some smaller skate species exhibit shorter lifespans, while larger deep-water species can exceed two decades at a temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C]. The conservative life-history strategy defined by these demographic parameters means that even moderate fishing mortality can substantially reduce the spawning stock biomass, and population models indicate that recovery from overfishing requires several decades under moratorium. Management measures such as minimum landing sizes and seasonal closures are designed to protect the mature segment of the population until they have had the opportunity to reproduce over several seasons, thereby sustaining the population over the long term. Continued monitoring of these demographic parameters is essential for adaptive fisheries management in the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean.
